1.pericope_label: Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, thou art very great; thou art clothed with honour and majesty. Who coverest thyself with light as with a garment: who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain

schools.summary: Delitzsch defines the psalm's whole character as a psalm of nature no Gentile poet could have written; Ellicott keeps the participles, makes light a continued operation rather than a past act, and refuses to limit the figure of the curtain.
Gill takes the light for the first created light and refers it to Christ; Calvin distinguishes the psalm from those of grace and turns the garment into an argument for God's visible glory.
Clarke supplies the titles from the versions and traces every image of the exordium to the tabernacle; Wesley refers the light to the first day's work.
Henry organises the whole opening as a royal progress — robes, palace, chariot, retinue; Spurgeon reasons from the placing of 'thou art very great' at the start rather than the end.
Augustine allegorises the opening throughout: the light is the church, and the heaven stretched like a skin is the authority of Scripture, dispensed through mortal men.

debates.question: What kind of psalm is this, and when was it written?

positions.summary: A psalm of nature such as no Gentile poet could have written, following the order of the creative beginnings in Genesis, where the psalm before sang the kingdom of grace.

Perhaps the principal poem in the collection and older than the Exodus, since it alludes neither to the Mosaic ritual nor to the deliverance from Egypt, and consists of parts sung alternately by two companies.
Untitled in the Hebrew and Chaldee but given to David by the versions, and so continuous with the psalm before that nine manuscripts write it as part of it.
So close a twin of the psalm before that it begins and ends the same way — when the model is perfect it deserves to exist in duplicate.

debates.question: Where does the imagery of the exordium come from?

positions.summary: From the tabernacle: the verb rendered 'put on' is the word used of the clothing of the priests, and the word rendered 'curtain' denotes the tabernacle's own curtains.
From tent, palace and temple together, with no need to limit so natural a figure to any one of them.
From the state of eastern kings — robes, palace and pavilion, coaches, retinue — beside whose equipage God's is as the sun to a glow-worm.

debates.question: What is the light God is clothed with?

positions.summary: The first created light, which expresses God's own nature and belongs to Christ.
The garment in which the God who dwells in inaccessible light appears visible to us, since he irradiates the world by his splendour.
Not a single past act of creation but a continued operation — the ethereal woof God is for ever weaving for his own wear.
The church, made light in him though darkness in herself.

outliers.summary: Argues from position: 'thou art very great' is the natural deduction from a survey of the universe and would have suited the end, so its standing first proves the whole psalm was digested before it was written.

themes: Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, thou art very great; thou art clothed with honour and majesty.
Who coverest thyself with light as with a garment: who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain:

3.pericope_label: Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters... Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again to cover the earth

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the deep as the primordial mass in which the earth lay as in embryo; Ellicott supplies the architectural vocabulary, denies that chaos appears in the poem at all, and reads the Hebrew dread of the sea into the coastline.
Gill canvasses the candidates for the earth's bases and settles on the power of God, and keeps the received sense of the angels.

Clarke keeps finding the tabernacle behind the imagery, explains the sea's bound by tides, rotation and gravitation, and doubts the mechanics of mountain springs; Wesley states the earth's suspension as a physical wonder.
Spurgeon reads the fleeing waters as intelligent agents obeying a word that can equally restrain the floods of trouble.

debates.question: Does the fourth verse speak of angels or of winds?

positions.summary: Of winds and lightnings: rather 'who maketh winds his messengers, a flaming fire his ministers', since the context deals throughout with the divine King's use of natural forces.
Of angels, created spirits by whom Christ's superiority is proved — though some render it 'as the winds'.
Of angels, incorporeal that they may be the fitter for their employments and called fire for their force.
Of the elements, prompt to perform the divine commands like ministers serving in the tabernacle.

debates.question: How do the waters go up by the mountains?

positions.summary: The received rendering is grammatically possible but inconsistent; better to make hills and valleys the subjects — hills rise, valleys sink — anticipating, in a different sense, geology.
By rain or arrested cloud sinking until stopped by solid strata, or by vapours condensed on the heights; water can hardly ascend through fissures to a summit.
The waters climb as clouds and descend as rain, equally willing either way.

debates.question: How is the earth's stability to be understood?

positions.summary: Better 'he fixed the earth on its foundations'; that this contradicts Job's 'he laid the earth upon nothing' need cause no difficulty, both being poetical, not scientific.
By the almighty power of God rather than by waters, centre of gravity, mountains or air.
As physical paradox: a heavy body so placed that whichever way it stirred it must fall upwards, and can be ruined only by tumbling into heaven.
By the tabernacle's pattern, so laid that nothing could move it until its purpose was accomplished.

outliers.summary: Observes that the idea of a chaos finds no place in the psalm's conception of the world's genesis: the primitive world is not formless but already has its mountains and valleys, merely merged beneath the sea.
Reads the coastline as evidence of the Hebrew dread of the sea — never an object of enjoyment, recreation or commerce, but simply the defence God has set against hostile waters.

themes: Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind:
Who maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire:
Who laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be removed for ever.
Thou coveredst it with the deep as with a garment: the waters stood above the mountains.
At thy rebuke they fled; at the voice of thy thunder they hasted away.
They go up by the mountains; they go down by the valleys unto the place which thou hast founded for them.
Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again to cover the earth.

10.pericope_label: He sendeth the springs into the valleys, which run among the hills... The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies

schools.summary: Ellicott contrasts the psalm's method with the Genesis narrative, corrects prepositions and renderings, and identifies the animals from natural history.
Gill spiritualises the wine and derives the wild goats' name from climbing.

Clarke supplies the physical science — evaporation, the proportion of sea to land, the effects of wine, oil and bread — and draws the lesson that no part of creation is useless; Wesley glosses the wild asses and the oil.
Henry grounds the springs in God as first cause and presses the moral that even useless creatures are welcome to their drink.

positions.summary: By evaporation on a fixed proportion — about seventeen parts of water to three of land, which is what the globe actually shows.
Naturalists dispute the second causes, but whatever they are, God is the first: there is water enough in the sea to drown us and not a drop to refresh us.

debates.question: What does 'herb for the service of man' mean?

positions.summary: For his use — though the Hebrew properly means labour, and some render it of man's labour in bringing the herb out of the earth, which the parallelism forbids.
Plants and nutritive grain generally, in whose germination there is a profusion of miracles.

debates.question: Whose are the trees that are full of sap?

positions.summary: Trees of field and forest, under God's cultivation rather than man's.
The cedars, grandest tree known to the Hebrew: man could grow herbs but not cedars, so these must have been planted by the divine hand.
Whoever planted the seeds of the cedars of Lebanon, or of the thousands of forests on the globe? God sowed them, and they flourished without the care of man.

outliers.summary: Notes that where Genesis passes from dry land straight to vegetation with no physical means of production, the Oriental poet thinks first of the springs on which life depends, and hastens — against the original record — to people his world with creatures who share the Creator's joy.

Distinguishes wine from ardent spirits, which exhilarate but exhaust, and observes that a little bread restores strength before it can have been prepared for nutriment — an effect he says has never been satisfactorily accounted for.

themes: He sendeth the springs into the valleys, which run among the hills.
They give drink to every beast of the field: the wild asses quench their thirst.
By them shall the fowls of the heaven have their habitation, which sing among the branches.
He watereth the hills from his chambers: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works.
He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth;
And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man’s heart.
The trees of the Lord are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted;
Where the birds make their nests: as for the stork, the fir trees are her house.
The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies.

19.pericope_label: He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down... O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches

schools.summary: Delitzsch shows the poet keeping the order of the creation days; Ellicott contrasts the poem's living luminaries with the mechanical account in Genesis and finds the curse of labour absent from the psalm altogether.
Gill collects the Jewish explanations of the moon's priority and the natural history of the lion.
Clarke sets out the alternation of labour and rest between man and beast, and reads the closing exclamation as three propositions with a moral conclusion.
Henry turns the luminaries against their worshippers and finds darkness a foil to the beauty of the day; Spurgeon presses the punctuality of the sun as evidence of appointment rather than law.

debates.question: Why is the moon named before the sun?

positions.summary: Because the poet wishes the picture of the day to follow that of the night, the moon being the calendrical principal star.
Partly from its importance in fixing the calendar, partly from the reckoning that makes evening and morning a day.
Because the night was before the day, and the moon measures months, years, tides and the appointed festivals.

debates.question: What is the point of naming sun and moon at all?

positions.summary: To show against their worshippers that they are creatures dependent on God and made for man's use.
To present them as conscious servants of God rather than mechanical timepieces, unlike the scientific manner of Genesis.
To forbid us to regard their motions as the result of impersonal law rather than divine appointment.

outliers.summary: Observes that the curse of labour on which Genesis dwells is entirely out of sight here, replaced by the poetry of labour, and that the later curse of overworked modern generations has not appeared either.
Reports that the lion is neither swift nor of good scent, and that on credible accounts a jackal little bigger than a fox hunts its prey and holds it until the lion comes up.

themes: He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down.
Thou makest darkness, and it is night: wherein all the beasts of the forest do creep forth.
The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their meat from God.
The sun ariseth, they gather themselves together, and lay them down in their dens.
Man goeth forth unto his work and to his labour until the evening.
O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches.

25.pericope_label: So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable... Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless thou the Lord, O my soul. Praise ye the Lord

schools.summary: Ellicott reconstructs the poet's standpoint and nationality from the sea and the ships, distinguishes the hidden face from displeasure, warns against reading later doctrine into 'spirit', and defends the closing imprecation as a necessary discord.
Gill reads the Hebrew idiom of the sea, refers the spirit to the Holy Spirit and the succession of creatures, and restricts the sinners to the notorious.

Clarke reads the renewal as a resurrection of the brute creation, explains the kindled hills by volcanoes, and turns the imprecation into a prediction; Wesley traces the first and last occurrence of the closing word.
Henry contrasts God's unfailing pleasure in his works with our regret over our own; Spurgeon rests the divine glory on God's being rather than his works.

debates.question: What does 'thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created' mean?

positions.summary: Breath, not the later doctrine of the Spirit: the vivifying power that gives matter a distinct but transient existence.
Not the first creation but the continued production of living creatures, 'created' taken in its largest sense.
The Holy Spirit, and the succession of creatures in the room of those that die.
A resurrection of the bodies that have been dissolved, the brute creation principally intended, when it is delivered from its bondage.
The whale or any large marine animal; the Greek and Latin call it a dragon.
In Job the crocodile, but here evidently of the sea and probably the whale.
The whale.

debates.question: How is the closing imprecation to be taken?

positions.summary: As a necessary discord: national feeling could not be absent from an Israelite hymn, and the song of creation would be false if no discord were heard, the harmony having been broken by sin.
Not as a wish but a prediction — God shall consume the wicked till no more be found.
Of the notorious sinners only, not of all who sin.

outliers.summary: Argues that death is to this poet neither sorrow nor mystery, since only the individual dies while the race lives — one generation fading as the breath is withdrawn and another succeeding as it is sent forth.
Reads the ships as evidence that the poet had seen the navies of Phoenicia and belonged to northern Palestine, and hears here for once a breath of enthusiasm for the sea.

themes: So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts.
There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein.
These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season.
That thou givest them they gather: thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good.
Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust.
Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.
The glory of the Lord shall endure for ever: the Lord shall rejoice in his works.
He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth: he toucheth the hills, and they smoke.
I will sing unto the Lord as long as I live: I will sing praise to my God while I have my being.
My meditation of him shall be sweet: I will be glad in the Lord.
Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless thou the Lord, O my soul. Praise ye the Lord.
